rv.q: Ultimately, the political message speaks loudest, harnessing the McCarthyist fear of then and the Trumpian terror of today.
Sharrock’s production is engaging rather than exciting.
It is mostly a strange mess, enjoyable but overloaded with baggage and suffering from sub-par ensemble work, the more noticeable stacked against the strength of Gough, Salazar, Crudup and Howle.
In the end, though, Roth doesn't quite persuade you that this is a story that needs to be remade.
Yet this world premiere tries on too many theatrical forms for size to find its own identity.
High Noon the play is an entertaining curio.
The evening has its moments, but as drama it’s slow on the draw.
Thea Sharrock’s production misses the sense of the small town’s vulnerability, all alone in the wide-open spaces of the dusty Midwest.
As the hands on that clock finally approach 12, what you’re chiefly left thinking is, what a waste of talent – and what a waste of time.
Not a total misfire, then, but it doesn’t hit the mark – better to re-watch the film.
Much as I hate to say it, save your money and watch the film instead.

What earns the final star above is not the adaptation’s subtle relevance nor its urgent pacing but the fact that though there’s an inevitable corniness to the plot, some 73 years after the film’s release, I was moved.
Eric Roth’s version and Thea Sharrock’s direction have a similar relevance to the world in this time of Donald Trump.
High Noon is a gripping, high-stakes play that transforms a powerful film into a suspenseful live experience.
The rest is careful and elegantly enjoyable, but lacks that emotional punch.
But for all the elegant shifts in light and shade and haze on view before us, the play only intermittently snaps into focus: less High Noon than a middling evening.
That forms an appropriate conclusion to a stage adaptation that itself feels like bloodless play-acting.
The total absence of suspense from this good-looking show is probably deliberate.
What a shame then that the idea to have the play deliver its story in real time, falls flat and ultimately proves more mule, than stallion.
Sadly, it misses the target like a gunslinger shooting blind.
That tension I mentioned might have been tighter with a clock chime now and then.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this stage adaptation of the classic western, with critics questioning its theatrical necessity. Billy Crudup earns praise, but Eric Roth's script is deemed wooden and the Trump-era allegory heavy-handed.
